respuesta:
I drew three recursion metaphors: a fractal tree (each stem sprouts two smaller rotated copies), nested squares that rotate and shrink inward, and a Sierpinski triangle of self-similar holes. Together they mean: reduce the problem to smaller copies of itself. The side arrows hint at a call that returns.

I considered a spiral (reads as a loop), nested dolls (muddy at this size), stacked frames (looks like a chart), a Y-combinator sketch (too obscure), and an ouroboros (cycles, not divide-and-conquer). Fractals were the clearest wordless signal.

I need to explain what the SVG symbol depicts, why I chose it, and what alternative designs I considered and rejected.

The SVG shows nested rectangles rotating and scaling inward, plus a Sierpinski-like triangle fractal. These patterns represent recursive self-similarity. I discarded simpler symbols like arrows or circles because they would not clearly convey the recursive strategy.

The symbol also contains a recursive tree structure and curved arrows pointing back to earlier elements. These elements together form a binary tree fractal, reinforcing the recursive strategy.

The branching lines form a self-similar tree where each node spawns two scaled, rotated copies. The nested squares shrink toward the center. The Sierpinski triangle shows holes filled with smaller triangles. These patterns together scream "reduce to smaller copies of the same problem." The side arrows suggest a call that returns. I wanted a symbol that instantly reads "recursion" without text.

I rejected a spiral because it suggests iteration. Nested Russian dolls are unreadable at this scale. A stack of frames looks like a bar chart. The Y combinator is too obscure. An ouroboros reads as cycles rather than divide-and-conquer. Fractals are the clearest language-free signal.
